messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
Kiet Pham is a 77-year-old Vietnamese American man, married and still working part-time as a firefighter in a mid-sized Midwestern city — a role he has held, in one form or another, for nearly four decades. He presented for psychological evaluation after his wife of fifty-one years told him, with quiet desperation, that she no longer recognized the man she had married. His PCL-5 score of 40 places him in the moderate-to-severe range, and the clinical picture that emerged across intake and early sessions is one of a man caught in a tightening loop he has neither the language nor the permission to name.

Kiet was eleven years old when the bombing began in his village in the Mekong Delta. He describes a morning that started like any other — the smell of cook-fire smoke, the sound of his younger sister calling his name — and then a concussive blast that seemed to erase the air itself. A neighboring family was killed. Kiet was thrown from his feet. When he found his footing again, there was blood on his hands that was not his own, and the name his sister had been calling echoed in the sudden silence. He does not speak of this at length. What he offers comes in fragments, and the fragments are vivid — startlingly so. His memories of that morning are exceptionally clear and detailed, he says, more like a film he is forced to watch than something that happened to a child sixty-six years ago. That quality of vividness is itself part of the burden: the memory forces its way into his mind without invitation, arriving whole and uninstructed. And yet, in the same breath, he will say that it feels like it happened to someone else — that the boy in the memory cannot be him, cannot be continuous with the man sitting in the chair across from the clinician. This dissociative quality does not diminish the intrusions; it makes them stranger and harder to metabolize.

In his work as a firefighter, the triggers are unavoidable. When an ambulance passes the station with its siren cycling through its lower registers, or when a controlled burn produces a percussion that carries across the yard, Kiet feels the morning return before he has consciously registered the sound. The name of a colleague — a young man named Minh, the same name as the neighbor killed in the blast — is enough to stop him mid-sentence. These sensory encounters do not merely recall the memory; they seem to unlock it, and the unlocking arrives alongside a particular shame. He had come to believe, in the months since symptoms intensified, that a stronger man — a smarter man — would not have been standing in that street. Someone else would not have gotten into this situation. The triggers do not only produce intrusions; they confirm his worst self-assessment, and that assessment, once activated, sends him scanning the firehouse and the surrounding block for signs of threat he cannot name but cannot stop looking for.

The negative appraisals have a way of generating their own dangers. When Kiet believes he is fundamentally diminished — that he feels like an object moved by events rather than a person who acts — he becomes hypervigilant to any stimulus that might confirm it, and the very act of scanning sharpens his sensitivity to the sounds and names that trigger him most. He had also come to believe, with a certainty that frightened him, that if he allowed himself to think about the event directly, something in him would break irreparably. This conviction drove him to avoid sleep and lying in the dark, where the memory found him most reliably. He began staying up until two or three in the morning, watching television with the volume low, and his wife began sleeping in the guest room. The sleep deprivation that followed did not quiet the memories — it made them more insistent, more vivid, and the exhaustion made his appraisals of himself crueler and more absolute. He also found himself, in unguarded moments, constructing elaborate revenge fantasies directed at figures from that morning — a habit that briefly relieved the helplessness but ultimately reinforced his sense that he remained trapped in something unresolved.

What finally brought Kiet to seek help was not his wife's plea, though that mattered. It was a shift at the firehouse three months ago when, upon hearing a controlled detonation from a construction site two blocks away, he dropped to the ground in front of three junior colleagues. He felt, he said, like a thing that had been knocked over. He is most afraid that nothing can be done. He is most hoping, tentatively and without much conviction, that he might be wrong about that.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: No paragraph establishes that Kiet's maladaptive strategies (e.g., sleep avoidance, staying up late, revenge fantasies) causally lead to or intensify the intrusive memory itself — the vignette notes sleep deprivation made memories 'more insistent and vivid,' but this is framed as a consequence of sleep deprivation rather than of the avoidance strategy driving the memory.
  e.g. "She had been avoiding any mention of it for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been — all that suppression had kept it fresh."
  e.g. "Not talking about it meant the memory had never been put anywhere; it remained in her, undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left it."
  e.g. "The effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close — she had thought about not thinking about it every day for three years."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph clearly conveys that Kiet's maladaptive strategies (avoidance, revenge fantasies, safety behaviours) causally produce or worsen his negative appraisals — the vignette mentions the revenge fantasies 'reinforced his sense of being trapped' but does not link the broader set of maladaptive strategies to generating or intensifying the negative self-appraisals (e.g., feeling diminished, blaming himself for being in the street).
  e.g. "Three years of avoiding it had told her something she couldn't easily argue with: that she must be more fragile than other people, or she would have been over this by now."
  e.g. "Each time she used a safety behaviour to get through the day, she felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that she couldn't cope without it."
  e.g. "The fact that she still needed to do all of this — the checking, the planning, the long way round — confirmed, in some wordless way, that she wasn't getting better."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
He began staying up until two or three in the morning, watching television with the volume low, and his wife began sleeping in the guest room. The sleep deprivation that followed did not quiet the memories — it made them more insistent, more vivid, and the exhaustion made his appraisals of himself crueler and more absolute.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
What Kiet had not understood was that the avoidance itself was doing part of the work of keeping the memory alive — by never allowing himself to sit with the morning in any deliberate way, he had ensured it remained unprocessed and intact, so that each night's evasion left it precisely as raw and immediate as the night before. The effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close; he had spent years thinking about not thinking about it, and the memory had stayed fresh in exactly the place he had refused to look.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
He also found himself, in unguarded moments, constructing elaborate revenge fantasies directed at figures from that morning — a habit that briefly relieved the helplessness but ultimately reinforced his sense that he remained trapped in something unresolved.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
More broadly, the accumulation of his avoidance strategies — the late nights, the deliberate skirting of anything that touched the event, the fantasies that substituted for genuine processing — had been quietly building a case against him that he could not rebut. Each morning he woke having once again managed not to confront the memory directly, the unspoken conclusion hardened: that a man who still needed all of this, after sixty-six years, must be exactly as diminished and culpable as he feared — that the boy who had been standing in that street had deserved what followed, and the old man still standing in its shadow deserved no better.
<<<END>>>
